units.translation: κόπανον [pestle], which properly means a pestle, on which see Thes. vol. 4 p. 1810, Aeschylus used of an axe. πειραί [the points], which the scholiast explains as πειραὶ αἱ ἀκμαὶ τῶν ξιφῶν, παρὰ τὸ πείρειν · κοπάνων δὲ τῶν κοπτικῶν ξύλων [the points are the edges of swords, from piercing; and of pestles, the cutting woods], is a word not otherwise known. For what is read in Diodorus in Exc. Vat. p. 48 ed. Mai. has been noticed by L. Dindorf in Thes. vol. 6 p. 669 to be corrupted from σπείραις [coils]. Nor should any weight be given to Lentz's conjecture (Herodian. vol. 1 p. 263, 14) who wanted to restore πειρά [trial] for the corrupt σχειρά [??] in Theognostus Can. p. 101, 24. Blomfield approved Pauw's conjecture πεῖραι [attempts], because it is said for πεῖραι κοπάνων μιανθέντων [attempts of defiled pestles], as Ag. 148 ἐκπατίοις ἄλγεσι παίδων [with out-of-the-way griefs of children] for ἐκπατίων ἄλγεσι παίδων [of out-of-the-way griefs of children]. But πεῖραι [attempts] is weaker than a word suitable for this passage and much less apt with the added words than πειραί [the points] in the meaning the scholiast took it.
the points are the edges of swords, from piercing; and of pestles, the cutting woods
With a genitive, as in Homer and others indicated in Thes. vol. 6 p. 675,
i.e. while the enemy are besieging the city,

unless, by removing the comma before and after δύνωμαι [I am able], πειράσομαι [I will try] is to be construed with ἐάν [if], as in Plato Leg. 1 p. 638 πειρώμενος ἂν ἄρα δύνωμαι δηλοῦν [trying if I can make clear].
try me as a woman without sense
to do for the gods while the enemy are trying
I will try, if I am able, to release you from these toils
I will try to meet my child
we will try to avert the pain of disease
I will try to rule the citizens
trying if I can make clear
Thus Schuetz for πισίμβροτόν τε βάκτρον [and the staff that persuades mortals].
fulfilling the fated lot with hands and with the staff that persuades mortals
and the staff that persuades mortals
Ιη Μπισμάτων σωτηρίου [??]. Corrected from the scholiast who noted ἀντὶ τοῦ πείς σματα σωτήρια [instead of saving cables]. More probable is σωτηρία [safety], which Turnebus restored.
breaths of ships and unsparing cables
who is in the deep (sea), marine.
He called the sea itself thus
as Dioscor. 5, 15 θαλάττης πελαγίας [of the sea, marine].
held the sea of the deep
near the salt sea of the deep
Improperly it is said of that which is immense, whence Hesychius explains it by μέγεθος, πλήθος [size, multitude].
they are neighbors of the Strymonian sea, the Acheloides
a stormy sea of ruinous misery
